You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 67
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Hotel Manager
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 62

# The Man Behind the Front Desk

Raymond is a 67-year-old married hotel manager who has spent the better part of four decades making sure other people feel safe. He knows the name of every bellhop, memorizes the preferences of returning guests, and can troubleshoot a double-booked suite at two in the morning without raising his voice. He has always taken quiet pride in that — in being the steady, unflappable presence at the center of a place that runs on the promise of comfort and security. That version of himself feels very far away now.

Fourteen months ago, Raymond was walking to his car after closing out the books on a late Tuesday shift. The hotel's parking structure was well-lit, the kind of place he had crossed a thousand times without a second thought. Two men approached him from behind a concrete pillar. One pressed what he believed was a gun into the small of his back. They took his wallet, his watch — a 40th anniversary gift from his wife, Carol — and his phone. The whole thing lasted perhaps ninety seconds. When it was over, Raymond sat on the oil-stained concrete for a long time before he could make himself stand up.

He told the police it was fine. He told Carol it was fine. He was back at work within two days, because the hotel needed him and because staying home felt worse than anything else he could imagine. But something had shifted in a way he couldn't name and couldn't undo.

The parking structure became impassable. Raymond now arrives before dawn and parks on the street, walking an extra four blocks in any weather, because the thought of entering that garage produces a sensation he describes as his heart trying to leave his chest. He has rerouted his entire daily life around a ninety-second event, and he knows it, and knowing it doesn't help.

Sleep is its own problem. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, sometimes mid-shout, sometimes just suddenly and completely awake with his pulse hammering and the absolute certainty that someone is in the room. Carol has learned not to touch him when this happens. He hates that she has learned that. He lies still in the dark and waits for his body to believe what his mind already knows — that he is in his own bed, that he is safe — and sometimes that takes an hour.

At work, Raymond finds himself watching. He clocks every person who enters the lobby, tracks where hands are, notices who lingers too long near the elevator bank. His assistant manager has gently mentioned that guests sometimes find him startling — that he appears to materialize beside them before they've seen him coming, as if he is always already on guard. He laughs this off. Inside, he understands exactly what he is doing. He is making sure no one gets close without him knowing first.

He has become short with Carol in ways that shame him. She asks a simple question and he hears an accusation. She reaches for him in the night and he flinches before he can stop himself. He has stopped going to their usual Saturday dinner with friends because restaurants feel loud and unpredictable and he can never find a seat with his back to the wall. Carol goes alone now, and she doesn't complain, and her patience frightens him more than her anger would.

What troubles Raymond most is not the fear itself but the gap it has opened between who he was and who he is now. He managed a hotel through two hurricanes, a kitchen fire, and a global pandemic. He prided himself on being the person others leaned on. Now he cannot walk through a parking garage. He cannot sleep through the night. He sits across from his wife at breakfast and feels, with a grief he doesn't have words for, like a stranger who has moved into his own life and doesn't quite know how to behave there.
